Customers.CustomerSummary: Customer A was a 76-year-old retiree whose investment objective was growth. Duggins recommended 120 transactions in Customer A's account from January 2019 through March 2022, resulting in an extremely high annualized cost-to-equity ratio of 93% and turnover rate of 20.55. This trading pattern caused $19,575 in realized losses and generated $32,331 in total trading costs, including $23,395 in commissions. The Care Obligation violation occurred as Duggins' excessive trading was clearly not in the customer's best interest given the senior investor's profile, particularly after Regulation BI went into effect on June 30, 2020. The violation is determined by the excessive quantitative metrics (turnover rate over 3x the guideline of 6 and cost-to-equity ratio nearly 5x the guideline of 20%) that indicated the customer needed to earn 93% annually just to break even.

Customer B was a 68-year-old retiree who opened an IRA with investment objective of aggressive growth. Duggins recommended 305 transactions in this retirement account from October 2018 through October 2021, resulting in an annualized cost-to-equity ratio of 59% and turnover rate of 14.82. This excessive trading caused $92,995 in realized losses and generated $123,953 in total trading costs, including $101,024 in commissions. The Care Obligation violation (starting from June 30, 2020) is evident from: 1) The quantitative metrics showing turnover rate more than 2x the excessive guideline of 6, 2) The cost-to-equity ratio nearly 3x the excessive guideline of 20%, 3) The recommendation of 305 transactions in a retirement account of a senior investor resulted in substantial losses, and 4) The customer needed to earn 59% annually just to break even on costs.

Customer C was a 42-year-old self-employed real estate professional with an investment objective of speculation. Duggins recommended 151 transactions in this account from September 2018 through November 2021, resulting in an annualized cost-to-equity ratio of 101% and turnover rate of 24.88. This excessive trading caused $17,829 in realized losses and generated $71,213 in total trading costs, including $55,195 in commissions. The Care Obligation violation is determined by: 1) The extremely high turnover rate more than 4x the excessive guideline of 6, 2) The cost-to-equity ratio more than 5x the excessive guideline of 20%, and 3) The customer would need to earn 101% annually just to break even on costs. Additionally, this customer later filed a written complaint against Duggins seeking $17,500 in damages due to excessive trading, which Duggins failed to disclose on his Form U4.

The case mentions five additional customers beyond the three detailed above, but does not provide specific information about each of these customers individually. Collectively, Duggins engaged in excessive trading across all eight customer accounts, with annualized cost-to-equity ratios ranging from 58% to 289% and annualized turnover rates ranging from 14.36 to 63.24. The total impact across all eight accounts was $444,176 in trading costs (including $343,416 in commissions) and $235,494 in realized losses. For these remaining five customers, Care Obligation violations would be similar to the pattern established with the first three customers - excessive trading that was not in their best interest.

Case Information.Type of Document: Letter of Acceptance, Waiver, and Consent (AWC)

OverallSummary: This case involves Tory A. Duggins willfully violating Regulation BI's Best Interest Obligation (specifically the Care Obligation) by recommending excessive trades to eight customers from December 2016 through April 2022, with particular emphasis on the period after Regulation BI went into effect on June 30, 2020. Three of the eight affected customers were seniors (ages 76, 68, and 42 identified). The Care Obligation violations were determined by applying quantitative metrics that far exceeded established guidelines: 1) Annualized cost-to-equity ratios ranged from 58% to 289% (far above the 20% threshold for excessiveness), 2) Annualized turnover rates ranged from 14.36 to 63.24 (far above the guideline of 6), 3) The trading generated $444,176 in total costs, including $343,416 in commissions, while causing $235,494 in realized losses across all accounts. The excessive trading was particularly egregious for the senior customers, with Customer A (76-year-old retiree) experiencing a 93% cost-to-equity ratio, Customer B (68-year-old retiree) experiencing a 59% cost-to-equity ratio in an IRA account, and Customer C having a 101% cost-to-equity ratio. Duggins exercised de facto control over these accounts as customers routinely followed his recommendations. The case also notes that Duggins willfully failed to report a written customer complaint alleging excessive trading, which constituted an additional violation. As a result of these violations, Duggins received an 18-month suspension, with no monetary sanctions due to demonstrated financial inability to pay.
